item.title: El-Sayed asked if he believes America is 'ready for a Muslim president' ahead of Senate race
item.description: Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed deflected questions about a presidential run, insisting his focus remains on winning the Michigan Senate race.
item.content:encoded:
Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed remarked on whether he would consider running for president of the United States, during an interview on NBC's "Meet the Press" Sunday.

Host Kristen Welker closed her interview asking El-Sayed whether he believed America was "ready" to elect a Muslim candidate for president.

"That's not a question I'm asking," El-Sayed answered. "I think Michigan is ready for a Muslim senator."

MICHIGAN DEM HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED JABS CNN GIVING HIM 'NON-CONSENSUAL COLONOSCOPY' IN RECENT INTERVIEWS

Welker repeated the question, but El-Sayed continued to say the question was "irrelevant" and that Michigan was ready for a Muslim senator.

"Okay, but you don't rule out the possibility that—?" Welker asked.

"I have no intention of ever running for president. That is not a thing I've ever wanted to do," El-Sayed said.

EL-SAYED TAUNTS TRUMP, CLAIMS HE'S GOING TO MAKE HIM 'MAIN CHARACTER OF THE MIDTERMS'

He continued, "I want to be a really great senator for my state. You know, someday, somewhere, somebody down the line decides to run, that would have been a really amazing thing to see how big America really is. But for right now, I really want to be the next senator from Michigan. That's what I’d like to be for a long time to come. I'm looking forward to serving out the next six years. I'm honored to get to do this. And look, America is a big place, and America has this incredible way of reminding us how big she really is. And that starts in Michigan."

During the interview, Welker also asked another question about a presidential run while referencing a reported comment made by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., where she remarked, "If Abdul can win in Michigan, anybody can win anywhere."

HARRIS JOINS FORCES WITH RADICAL SENATE NOMINEE IN KEY SWING STATE AS 2028 WHISPERS SWIRL

"If you lose Michigan, does that mean that a progressive like AOC can't win the White House in 2028?" Welker said.

"Look, this is one seat in Michigan that has a lot more to do with our local issues in Michigan than it has to do with a national referendum," El-Sayed said.

Fox News Digital reached out to NBC and El-Sayed's campaign for comment.

El-Sayed's interview came after his Thursday debate with GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers in which Rogers brought up alleged ties between El-Sayed and the Muslim Brotherhood terrorist organization.

El-Sayed has repeatedly denied these ties. He also rejected the premise when asked by Welker.

"No," he said, before claiming the allegation was based in Islamophobia.

"It's truly shameful, but he has no ideas, he doesn't actually care about solving problems," El-Sayed said of Rogers.

In a comment to Fox News Digital, Media Research Center President David Bozell criticized what he considered Welker's eagerness to consider El-Sayed a presidential candidate.

"NBC took one look at Abdul El-Sayed and started planning the presidential library. Never mind Hasan Piker. Never mind Michigan. Meet the Press skipped the vetting and went straight to measuring El-Sayed’s Oval Office drapes," Bozell said.

item.title: Aaron Rodgers defies Father Time with another three-touchdown performance in Steelers’ win
item.description: Aaron Rodgers threw three touchdowns as the Steelers beat the Colts 34-22, surpassing Peyton Manning for third in all-time touchdown passes.
item.content:encoded:
I thought Aaron Rodgers was cooked coming into the 2026 season, and his performances in the first two weeks did little to change my mind.

In my Week 2 takeaways column, I described him as "an old quarterback whose career probably should have ended three years ago."

Yeah, so, that assessment could use an update.

The 42-year-old threw three touchdown passes Sunday as the Pittsburgh Steelers beat the Indianapolis Colts, 34-22, to improve to 3-2. Rodgers finished with 235 passing yards and has now thrown three touchdowns in three consecutive games.

'WHAT THE F--K, CALL IT!': AARON RODGERS AND MIKE MCCARTHY CURSE AT EACH OTHER DURING HOT MIC MOMENT

Over that stretch, he's passed for 826 yards and nine touchdowns. That's pretty good production for anyone, let alone a quarterback who is likely playing in his final NFL season.

For comparison, Rodgers had more turnovers (2) than touchdown passes (1) in the first two games.

Now, he's still averaging one turnover per game after throwing three interceptions in the past three games, so he has to clean that up.

He didn’t turn the ball over Sunday, though, showing he's still got some football left in that 42-year-old right arm.

The encouraging part for Pittsburgh is that Rodgers is giving the offense something to build on each week.

Sunday's opening possession went backward, costing the Steelers 15 yards before they punted. But Rodgers responded quickly. On Pittsburgh's next possession, he got the ball to Jaylen Warren just before taking a hit from defensive tackle Grover Stewart, and Warren turned the short completion into an 80-yard touchdown.

Rodgers went on to complete his first 11 passes and didn't have an incompletion until midway through the second quarter.

Of course, Warren deserves plenty of credit for making his quarterback's numbers look better. He finished with 188 yards from scrimmage and added a 50-yard touchdown run to go with the long receiving score. That's a pretty productive afternoon.

JASON KELCE’S EAGLES-JAGUARS BROADCAST SHOWS WHY NFL BOOTHS COULD USE MORE OFFENSIVE LINEMEN

But Rodgers also delivered when Pittsburgh needed to put some distance between itself and Indianapolis.

With the Steelers leading 24-22 in the fourth quarter, Rodgers found Pat Freiermuth for a 17-yard touchdown on third-and-6. It was Freiermuth's second touchdown catch of the afternoon and basically locked up the victory.

There were a couple of historical accomplishments mixed in, too.

The touchdown pass to Warren moved Rodgers ahead of Peyton Manning for third in career touchdown passes, including the postseason. Only Tom Brady and Drew Brees remain ahead of him.

DRE GREENLAW'S SEAN PAYTON BEEF EXPOSES ANOTHER SIDE OF THE NFL'S MOST OVERRATED HEAD COACH

The victory also gave Rodgers 166 regular-season wins as a starting quarterback, moving him past Ben Roethlisberger into fifth place all time. Passing a Steelers legend while wearing a Steelers uniform is a nice bonus.

The career accomplishments are impressive, obviously. But Steelers fans have a more immediate interest in whether Rodgers can keep playing like this.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Pittsburgh needs an offense that can take advantage when its defense gets stops, finish drives with touchdowns and deliver a big play when a game gets uncomfortable. Rodgers and Warren gave the Steelers all of that against Indianapolis.

There's still plenty of season left, and three good games don't settle every question about this team. They're also in the very competitive AFC North, where all four teams have three wins already.

The upcoming schedule provides an opportunity for Rodgers and the Steelers to keep rolling. Pittsburgh plays at Tampa Bay in Week 6 and then faces New Orleans in Paris. The Buccaneers and Saints are a combined 2-8.

After that comes a pair of crucial division games against the Browns and Bengals with a bye week in between. It remains to be seen if Rodgers can keep up this level of production as the season wears on.

But after throwing nine touchdown passes in three games? Yeah, I probably buried Rodgers a little too soon.

item.title: Trump Russia deal could fuel Putin's war, ex-NATO commander warns as Zelenskyy says 'nyet'
item.description: Donald Trump's energy ceasefire could hand Vladimir Putin fresh revenue to fuel Russia's war in Ukraine, former NATO commander Breedlove warns.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump's efforts to reach a diesel agreement with Russia could provide Russian President Vladimir Putin with fresh revenue to fund his war against Ukraine while allowing Moscow to buy time through negotiations it has little intention of honoring, a former NATO commander warned Sunday.

Retired Gen. Philip Breedlove, former NATO supreme allied commander Europe and head of U.S. European Command, told Fox News Digital that Washington also risks undermining Ukraine's war effort by striking a deal with what he called "the enemy."

"And so we are cutting a deal with the enemy," Breedlove said, warning that "all of this money will go into fueling Mr. Putin's continued attacks in Ukraine."

The Russian government said Saturday it had partially lifted a ban on diesel exports with immediate effect, following the new agreement between Putin and Trump for Russia to supply the U.S. and global markets, Reuters reported.

As previously reported by Fox News Digital, Trump's package calls for the release of 300,000 tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace," followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another 1 million tonnes afterward.

KATIE ZACHARIA HITS GROUND RUNNING, PROMISES TRUMP DIESEL DEAL DELIVERS CHEAPER GAS FOR AMERICANS

The diesel agreement preceded Trump's announcement Sunday of what he called an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, with the president saying both sides had agreed to halt attacks on energy infrastructure.

"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, however, indicated that Ukraine had not been informed of a finalized ceasefire agreement but expressed willingness to halt attacks on Russian energy facilities if Moscow reciprocated. He also accused Putin of repeatedly rejecting peace proposals and continuing strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure.

"Ukraine has proposed many de-escalatory steps. Putin had one answer to all of them – 'nyet,'" Zelenskyy wrote on X.

"We do hope that he will finally say something to America, Ukraine, and the entire world that will lead to a real and dignified peace," he added.

Zelenskyy also said Russian forces had carried out more than 200 strikes on Ukraine's electricity generation and transmission facilities over the past week, along with 17 strikes targeting gas and oil infrastructure.

He said the attacks had killed more than 150 people and wounded more than 700 over the past week.

Trump's "energy ceasefire" announcement followed tension between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, a component of Ukraine's strategy to weaken Moscow's ability to finance its military campaign.

UKRAINE TARGETS RUSSIA WITH OVER 1,000 DRONES, KILLING 2 AS MOSCOW HOLDS LAST DAY OF ELECTIONS

Breedlove argued that Russia and Ukraine are pursuing different objectives, accusing Moscow of targeting Ukrainian civilians and critical infrastructure while describing Kyiv's attacks on Russian energy facilities as an effort to disrupt the revenue sustaining Putin's war.

"Russia is carrying on a campaign of what we call counter value. In other words, Russia is attacking the Ukrainian people and trying to force their society to separate themselves from their president, President Zelenskyy," Breedlove said.

Breedlove also predicted Washington would pressure Zelenskyy to suspend attacks on Russia's oil industry despite their strategic importance.

"What I expect will happen is the United States will force or try to force Zelenskyy to stop bombing the petrochemical business in Russia," he said.

TRUMP'S DIESEL IDEA COULD HAVE UNLEASHED A PROBLEM AMERICANS NEVER SAW COMING

Trump has vehemently criticized Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, arguing that they are disrupting global diesel supplies and driving up costs for American farmers and ranchers.

Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended the administration's efforts to increase diesel supplies.

"We're going to do it with all the legal authorities we have," Bessent said Sunday on Fox News. "This is good for the American people, bringing these diesel prices down," he said of the new deal.

Separately, appearing on ABC News' "This Week," Zelenskyy offered to organize Ukrainian elections if Putin agreed to a reciprocal 60-day ceasefire, although holding a vote would face legal and logistical obstacles under Ukraine's martial law.

Breedlove also expressed deep skepticism that Putin would honor any such ceasefire, citing what he described as a pattern of Russian attacks following negotiations with Trump. "Russia has never kept a promise to this president in this war," Breedlove said.

UKRAINE'S ATTACKS ON RUSSIA ARE PUSHING PUTIN CLOSER TO NEGOTIATING TABLE, TRUMP NATO AMBASSADOR SAYS

"He's never changed his expectations, and he's never delivered on his promises. Three out of four of the big cases, the very next day or that same night after the president and Mr. Putin talked, Mr. Putin launched huge attacks in Ukraine," Breedlove continued.

Breedlove also called for a tougher U.S. response.

"We now need an administration that leads from power. We say all the time, 'strength through power,' but when it comes to Russia, our demonstrated position is continued conflict through weakness," Breedlove warned.

"He started this war. This war is to benefit Russia, and this war is to keep Mr. Putin in power. And our administration needs to tell him to stop."

item.title: Three men found guilty of murdering Australian brothers and American friend on Mexico surfing trip
item.description: Prosecutors are seeking 210 years in prison for each defendant convicted in the murders of the Australian brothers and their American friend.
item.content:encoded:
Three men have been convicted in the brutal killings of two Australian brothers and their American friend, whose disappearance on a Mexico surf trip sparked an international search before their bodies were found dumped in a well.

A judge in Ensenada on Friday found Jesús Gerardo García, known as "El Kekas," Irineo Francisco "N," and Ángel Jesús "N," guilty of murdering Callum and Jake Robinson, along with their friend Carter Rhoad, in Baja, California, in April 2024, The Associated Press reported.

The men were also convicted of armed robbery and armed carjacking. Judge Raúl Hernández is scheduled to announce their sentences Oct. 16, with the Baja California State Attorney General’s Office seeking 210 years in prison for each defendant, according to the AP.

MINNESOTA FATHER CONVICTED OF KILLING TEENAGE SON WHOSE REMAINS WERE FOUND IN LANDFILL

The verdicts followed a month-long trial that included testimony about one victim pleading for his life before the killings.

García’s former partner, Ary Gisell Silva Raya, testified that he told her he approached the surfers’ tent carrying a 9mm pistol, the AP reported. The men threw their belongings toward him in an effort to stop the attack, and one begged to be spared, she said.

AMERICAN AIRLINES FLIGHT ATTENDANT'S ALLEGED KILLERS TIED TO GANG ACCUSED OF PREYING ON TOURISTS: OFFICIALS

According to her testimony, García ignored the plea.

The friends had traveled to Baja, California, to surf and were reported missing after arriving in Punta San Jose, about 50 miles from Ensenada. Their bodies were discovered in a well May 3, 2024.

MEXICAN SPORTS JOURNALIST ROBBED AT GUNPOINT DURING LIVE REPORT

Authorities initially said the men were killed after confronting thieves who wanted the tires from their pickup truck.

Chief state prosecutor María Elena Andrade Ramírez said at the time that investigators believed the thieves spotted the truck and tents, then encountered resistance from the surfers during the attempted theft.

García allegedly told his girlfriend he had done something to "three gringos" before admitting, "I killed them," according to the BBC’s account of a May 2024 court hearing.

She also said he showed her a vehicle fitted with tires allegedly stolen from the victims’ truck.

MAN ACCUSED OF KILLING PARTNER ARRESTED IN MEXICO NEARLY TWO YEARS AFTER FLEEING WITH THEIR TWO CHILDREN

Silva Raya was found with one victim’s cellphone. Prosecutors said she met the surfers April 27, 2024, and urged one of her companions to rob them, the AP reported.

She pleaded guilty to aggravated robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence and was sentenced to 20 years in prison in November 2025. García and the other two men went to trial.

JURY CONVICTS KEVIN SALAZAR IN EXECUTION-STYLE KILLING OF LA DEPUTY RYAN CLINKUNBROOMER

The guilty verdicts brought a measure of relief to the Robinson family more than two years after the brothers’ deaths.

Their father, Martin Robinson, described the decision as a significant moment in the family’s painful pursuit of justice, according to the AP. He said the outcome could not undo their loss but offered a step toward justice as they continued honoring the three men.

MAN PLEADS GUILTY TO 2023 KILLING OF LAUREN HEIKE ON PHOENIX HIKING TRAIL

The brothers’ mother, Debra Robinson, spoke about their love of surfing during a tribute on a San Diego beach shortly after their bodies were found.

"Our hearts are broken, and the world has become a darker place for us," she said at the time. "They were young men enjoying their passion of surfing together."

She recalled that Jake, a doctor, sought work at hospitals near surfing beaches and urged others to honor her sons by embracing life.

"Live bigger, shine brighter, and love harder in their memory," she said.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Ben Affleck says political 'hypocrisy, corruption and failure' left him 'disillusioned'
item.description: Ben Affleck calls U.S. politics "terrible" and "tawdry" while promoting "Animals," a new movie in which he plays an L.A. mayoral candidate.
item.content:encoded:
Ben Affleck has no interest in running for public office.

The "Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice" star told Variety that trying to become a politician sounds "terrible" and "tawdry" to him.

"I just think that’s enormously — I don’t know, man, that seems terrible," Affleck told the outlet while promoting a new movie in which he plays a candidate for L.A. mayor. "There’s a reason why political stories are often chosen as parables for moral compromise. You really get thrust up into the contrast between the ideal version of us and how we should be in our lives and the way it is."

BEN AFFLECK DIRECTS, STARS IN NETFLIX KIDNAPPING THRILLER 'ANIMALS' COMING THIS OCTOBER

The 54-year-old called politics a "very depressing world, in my opinion. Tawdry. And that has no appeal to me."

He also declined to tell the outlet who he was backing for mayor in Los Angeles this November.

"I haven’t thought about being asked that. I don’t know if, given this movie, my endorsement harms or helps anybody," he admitted. "I should stay agnostic, at least until the movie comes out."

Affleck told Good Morning America on Wednesday that he believes the "collective bar for politics because of the way the political world has sort of evolved has gotten so low that there’s this kind of like, you know, people are just sort of looking for like just ‘Somebody shoot me straight.’’"

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS WANT MAJOR CHANGE AMID ECONOMIC AND POLITICAL DISCONTENT

He added that there’s a sense in the country, whether you’re a Democrat or a Republican that "we’re not doing a very good job. We have a system that’s kind of failing us."

Playing a man running for mayor taught him: "This is not all that much fun. And it would be a hard way — you’re just raising money all the time."

NETFLIX DROPS FULL TRAILER FOR BEN AFFLECK'S 'ANIMALS' AND EXPECTATIONS ARE ALREADY SOARING

He said that he and the man playing his campaign manager in the movie decided one day to take campaign shirts and hats with the name of his character, go out in L.A. and claim he was running for mayor.

When he told people he was running as his character, Affleck said voters would ask for a selfie, they seemed interested and "people would launch into their whole thing and I was like ‘If I’m not careful, I’m going to win this.'"

MICHAEL RAPAPORT DOUBLES DOWN ON 2029 NYC MAYORAL RUN, VOWS 'STREET FIGHT' AGAINST ZOHRAN MAMDANI

"Do not vote for me for mayor!" he joked to the camera.

BILL MAHER REVEALS BEN AFFLECK REFUSED ‘REAL TIME’ RETURN AFTER STORMY APPEARANCE IN 2014 DEBATING ISLAM

Affleck called holding office an "awful job" in an interview with USA Today via The Sacramento Bee this week, adding that he’s "so disillusioned with the system and with politics and politicians, and the way it works."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

When told his campaign ad in the movie was good, he answered, "I'd be flattered, except I think there's such a low bar in politics these days."

Affleck explained that his movie "Animals" is about the moral compromises people make.

"The extremely effective nature of when a person individually has something to lose is when they're most apt to make compromises," he says. "Are we just kind of self-seeking animals who, in retrospect, build stories to rationalize where we are and what we've done? And there's another part of us, our sort of higher selves, which says, 'Well, I'm going to adhere this moral code even if there's a cost to me.'"

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

The actor has been politically active in the past, campaigning for candidates from former Vice President Al Gore to former President Barack Obama.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

But he said he’s now "averse" to the idea because he’s seen so much "hypocrisy, corruption and failure."

"The way it's constructed now is so geared around money, sound bites, cruelties and gotchas, and little snarky things that really have nothing to do with people's lives whatsoever," he said. "And increasingly, it's easier to get votes appealing to the worst in people than it is appealing to the best in them. If you're telling a story about kind of morality and compromise, there are lots of pressures that are constantly asking you to sacrifice your principles."

item.title: Quiet part out loud: Anti-Israel mobs want one state called 'Palestine,' erasing Israel
item.description: Three pro-Palestinian activists tell Fox News Digital they envision replacing Israel with a single democratic state, with one proposing the name "1948."
item.content:encoded:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — This weekend, millions of anti-Israel activists marched through the streets of cities in coordinated actions from America's capital to London, Paris, Madrid and Kuala Lumpar, Malaysia, chanting the familiar refrains of "Free, free Palestine" and "From the river to the sea, Palestine will be free."

But for the first time, communicated frankly in exclusive interviews with Fox News Digital, three anti-Israel leaders acknowledged the goal: one state called "Palestine" encompassing modern-day Israel, the West Bank and Gaza, with a Palestinian "right of return" to the new country and equal political, voting and citizenship rights for Palestinians alongside Jews currently living in Israel.

Most significantly, in the political vision they described, Israel would legally cease to exist as a separate Jewish nation-state and Jews would be quickly overwhelmed demographically.

INSIDE THE PROTEST PLAYBOOK TO VILIFY ISRAEL ON 'GLOBAL DAY OF ACTION'

The current population of Israel is about 10 million, including about 7.8 million Jews, 2 million Palestinian Arabs (including Palestinians and most of them Muslim), and 200,000 people from other communities. There are another estimated 10.2 million Jews worldwide.

There are about 5.5 million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza and about 8 million Palestinians in the diaspora, totaling about 13.5 million.

The candor of the anti-Israel leaders lays bare the political conclusion of an argument that activists have spent years advancing on the streets, through sympathetic media outlets and in legal forums: that Israel is a "settler colonial" state practicing "apartheid" and "genocide," and therefore should not continue to exist in its current form as a Jewish state. Israeli leaders have fiercely rejected those allegations, disputing accusations of "genocide" and "apartheid" and maintaining that Israel is the nation-state of the Jewish people with equal civil and political rights for citizens that include Jews, Christians and Muslims.

Advocates for Israel note that the nation's critics rarely apply the same historical lens of human-rights analysis to Arab and Muslim-majority states, many of which emerged from the collapse of empires, wars and population upheavals that displaced millions, including Jews expelled from their countries, today often restricting political, religious and minority rights.

NOBEL PEACE PRIZE AWARDED TO UN JURIST WHO ACCUSED ISRAEL OF COMMITTING GENOCIDE IN GAZA

In Chicago, Hatem Abudayyeh, the Palestinian-American founder of the U.S. Palestinian Community Network and a Muslim, said the new nation would be "one democratic secular state of Palestine." Jewish Israeli-born community leader Miko Peled, founder of the Palestine House in Washington, D.C., said "the proper name would be Palestine." And Maryland congressional candidate Sam Husseini, a Palestinian-American Christian, floated another name for the vision of the one state: "1948," marking the year Israel declared independence and Palestinians commemorate as the "Nakba," or catastrophe, but he said even Israeli Jews would one day accept another name: "Palestine."

Their answers provide a striking interpretation from inside a movement where activists have traditionally danced around their demands with euphemisms about "liberation" and media outlets have obscured their answers even when they have been transparent.

On Washington, D.C.'s First Avenue SE, Fox News Digital asked Olivia DiNucci, local coordinator for CodePink, a far-left nonprofit, what her group sees as a solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. In her work for CodePink, DiNucci disrupts hearings, restaurant meals and town halls to shout at lawmakers and policymakers who support the state of Israel.

‘TROJAN HORSES’ IN AMERICA: CONGRESS PROBES INFLUENCE NETWORKS TIED TO CHINA, IRAN AND CUBA

"Palestinians in Palestine will decide, DiNucci said.

Asked if "Palestine" includes modern day Israel, she spun around and walked away. Later, she posted a message on social media, saying she was asked "gotcha questions."

This weekend, protesters signaled their position with certainty, explicitly rejecting the two-state solution that has dominated international diplomacy for decades.

In New York City, the Party for Socialism and Liberation circulated video of protesters marching through the streets chanting: "1-2-3-4. Occupation no more. 5-6-7-8. Israel is a terrorist state."

ISRAEL, JEWS TARGETED WORLDWIDE AS WELL-FUNDED LEFTIST, ISLAMIST GROUPS JOIN FOR ‘NAKBA 78’ PROTESTS

Then came the point: "We don't want no two state!"

In London, the Palestine Solidarity Campaign promoted a 15-second video of a woman with a megaphone shouting: "There is only one state!"

"Palestine, '48!" protesters responded.

"Say it loud, say it clear!" she continued. "Palestine, you make us proud!"

Back in Washington, D.C., protesters carried signs declaring, "LAND YOU HAVE 2 KILL FOR IS NOT YOURS," a message that challenged Israel's claim to the land itself, while a banner proclaiming, "THE FIGHT FOR LIBERATION IS OURS," framed the struggle as one for the territory. The demonstrators yesterday didn't address the Hamas attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, but many have called them justified.

ANTI-ISRAEL GROUPS RALLY ACROSS US ON OCTOBER 7 ANNIVERSARY, CHANTING 'LONG LIVE THE INTIFADA'

The one-state demand is being amplified within a powerful protest infrastructure. The broader "red-green" alliance brings socialist and communist groups together on the streets with Palestinian and Muslim activist organizations, while organizations including the Democratic Socialists of America and nonprofits in the network funded by Neville Roy Singham, an American-born tech tycoon living in Shanghai, help organize, promote and amplify anti-Israel demonstrations.

Singham, has poured $278 million into a pro-communist network, including CodePink, the People's Forum, the Party for Socialism and Liberation, BreakThrough News and the ANSWER Coalition, which have become major organizing, media and logistical hubs for the protest movement. The result is a powerful infrastructure amplifying slogans such as "Free Palestine" and "from the river to the sea," even when the organizations and activists doing the amplifying don't themselves explicitly spell out the one-state political vision described to Fox News Digital.

From Chicago, Abudayyeh told Fox News Digital that the U.S. Palestinian Community Network advocates for one democratic state across the territory that today encompasses Israel, the West Bank and Gaza.

"Our points of unity, from the very beginning of our existence, included one democratic secular state of Palestine," he said.

"And for decades and decades, we've been saying that...the only true solution that can bring peace and justice to all that live there is ... one democratic state," which includes the West Bank, Gaza and "1948 Palestinian territories," a term used to describe the land that Israel claimed as a nation in 1948.

This can only happen, he said, if "the racist system of Zionism is dismantled."

The ADL, a leading Jewish organization based in New York, describes Zionism as a "movement for the self-determination and statehood for the Jewish people in their ancestral homeland, the land of Israel."

Abudayyeh said the new state would include a "right of return" for Palestinian refugees and their descendants. "Our points of unity from day one included the right of return," he said.

Activists from a U.S.-based network of groups called "Al-Awda: The Palestine Right to Return Coalition" joined the protest in Los Angeles and posted a message online: "OUR PEOPLE WILL RETURN, PALESTINE WILL BE FREE!

"If all of our refugees, who have the internationally recognized right to return to Palestine, are able to return, and the system, the racist system is dismantled, then all the people there can live in peace and justice," Abudayyeh told Fox News Digital. "That's our position. It's always been our position. We're not going to abandon the five to seven million refugees that we have."

"They have the right to go back to the homes and lands in which they were exiled," he explained.

Abudayyeh said that wouldn't mean removing the people – most of them Jewish – living in Israel.

"It doesn't mean that we're going to kick people out," he said. "It just means that these folks have an internationally recognized right, and you will never get peace and justice there unless you uphold that right."

"I believe, very clearly, USPCN believes very clearly that there can be peace and justice as long as that system, that racist system of Zionism is dismantled," Abudayyeh said. "That's the essence of it."

Abudayyeh compared the Palestinian movement's objective to the international campaign against apartheid South Africa. "And we're getting close to having international consensus today on the question of Israel and Zionism, where Israel doesnt have the "right to exist as a racist, Zionist, apartheid, white supremacist state."

"That's what we say," he continued. "We're adamant about that. We're clear about it. Unabashed."

Fox News Digital asked Abudayyeh whether "Palestine" includes modern-day Israel when protest leaders and activists chant "Palestine will be free" or "Free, free Palestine."

"The majority of the majority of the people, especially in the past period, have moved to that conclusion," Abudayyeh said.

Husseini, a Palestinian-American journalist running for Congress in Maryland's 4th Congressional District, offered a similar one-state vision and an unusual proposal for what the country might be called.

Standing on First Avenue SE, between the U.S. Supreme Court and the U.S. Capitol, Husseini told Fox News Digital that his long-term vision is "one person, one vote," coupled with a Palestinian right of return.

"Ultimately, long-term, I that it should be one person, one vote," Husseini said.

"Why aren't they allowed back into their homes? So I think that they should," he said of Palestinian refugees. "I mean, that includes myself. I don't know that I would actually move back there, but as a descendant of a Palestinian who was forcibly displaced, I should have that right or compensation."

Husseini offered another possibility for the country's name.

"I've often thought of a novel proposal because people get hung up on the names. Are they going to call it Israel or are they going call it Palestine?" Husseini said.

"I've toyed with the idea of calling it 1948, having a country with a number signifying the year of this cataclysm, which should be the last gasp of imperialism."

If the new state is called Palestine, Husseini said, "I think a lot of Jews, when they think about it, will say, so long as they have equal rights and all are protected, will adopt the term Palestine."

Standing on Pennsylvania Avenue SE, the roar of the demonstrators getting closer as they marched from the U.S. Capitol to talks at the Palestine House of Freedom, Miko Peled, an Israeli-born Jewish activist, was equally blunt about what a "Free Palestine" means to him.

"Well, our vision, our mission, and our vision is to educate people to see that a free Palestine, which means a post-Zionist, post-apartheid Palestine with equal rights and the right of the Palestinians to return, is the best vision that will benefit everybody who lives there currently, which means Israelis and Palestinians," he said.

Asked whether that meant one state, he answered yes.

"It's already one state, it's just an apartheid state," Peled said.

"So that's our vision, to create a real democracy, free Palestine, with equal rights."

Fox News Digital asked what that country would be called.

"Well, historically the country was called Palestine for thousands of years and so it should be called Palestine," Peled said. "Israel is a new name. They renamed the country 78 years ago, so the proper name would be Palestine."

For Peled, the familiar protest demand "Free Palestine" has a literal political meaning: One state with the new name "Palestine."

item.title: Hidden clues could help predict a woman’s breast cancer risk years in advance
item.description: An AI tool developed at NYU Langone Health analyzes years of 3D mammograms to predict breast cancer risk up to five years before a diagnosis.
item.content:encoded:
An artificial intelligence (AI) tool could help doctors predict a woman's risk of developing breast cancer years in advance, according to new research.

In a new study, published in the American Journal of Roentgenology, researchers at NYU Langone Health and its Perlmutter Cancer Center tested an AI model designed to estimate a woman's risk of developing breast cancer within five years.

The tool looks at several years of a woman's 3D mammograms to track changes in breast tissue over time, rather than looking only at the latest scan, according to the researchers.

NEW ALZHEIMER'S BLOOD TEST PREDICTS WHO IS LIKELY TO DEVELOP DEMENTIA IN 5 TO 10 YEARS

The model was developed using more than 313,000 mammograms from more than 161,000 women, according to the study.

Connie Lehman, a Massachusetts-based breast imaging specialist and professor of radiology at Harvard Medical School who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital that AI could help identify women whose increased risk might otherwise go unnoticed.

"For decades, as a doctor and breast imaging specialist, I have cared for women who were shocked by a breast cancer diagnosis," Lehman said. "Again and again, I heard: 'How can this be? No one in my family has had breast cancer.'"

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Traditional risk assessments can consider factors such as family history and genetic mutations, while AI can look for additional clues within a woman's breast tissue, according to Lehman.

"A mammogram can tell us more than whether cancer is visible today — it can also provide information about a woman's risk of developing cancer in the years ahead," she said.

That information could eventually help doctors tailor breast cancer screening to a woman's individual risk, Lehman said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

Women identified as being at increased risk could discuss additional screening, such as MRI, with their health care providers, while women at average risk may continue with routine mammograms, according to Lehman.

The technology could also analyze mammograms a woman has already had, meaning the added risk information would not require another imaging exam or additional radiation, she noted.

Lehman cautioned that an AI risk score is not a cancer diagnosis and cannot predict with certainty whether a woman will develop the disease.

"A higher score can prompt a conversation with your health care provider about additional screening and risk-reduction options," she said. "A lower score does not eliminate risk or replace regular mammography."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The NYU model remains a research tool and is not FDA-authorized for clinical use, according to Lehman.

The researchers also noted that more testing is needed. The study used mammograms from NYU Langone hospitals and imaging equipment from one manufacturer.

The team plans to test the model using data from other medical centers and different 3D mammography systems, according to NYU Langone.

Fox News Digital reached out to the researchers for comment.

item.title: Lane Kiffin is staring down disastrous year one as offseason pleas for patience fall on deaf ears
item.description: Lane Kiffin's $40 million LSU Tigers roster faces mounting pressure after a stunning 35-34 loss to Will Stein's Kentucky Wildcats at Kroger Field.
item.content:encoded:
One of the biggest, most consequential games of the season so far took place in Tuscaloosa on Saturday night — in the wake of a hurricane, no less — but a different game was taking place about six hours north on I-65 that was also rife with national implications.

The Kentucky Wildcats and LSU Tigers played an all-time classic of a college football game this weekend, with Big Blue Nation pulling off a stunner, downing the top-ten Tigers 35-34 in front of a sold-out crowd at Kroger Field.

What this means for the Wildcats and first-year head coach Will Stein can't be overstated, as the new Kentucky head man now has two top-ten wins in his first six games on the job, and the arrow is pointing straight up in the Bluegrass State as of mid-October.

KENTUCKY COACH WILL STEIN TELLS WILDCATS PLAYERS 'IF YOU DON'T BELIEVE IN WHAT WE'RE DOING, YOU ARE HIGH'

But on the opposite sideline on Saturday night, LSU head coach Lane Kiffin was left with more questions than answers as the honeymoon phase in Baton Rouge likely came to a screeching halt.

Things aren't exactly up in smoke for Kiffin in his first year on the Bayou.

LANE KIFFIN KNOWS THERE AREN’T EXCUSES AT LSU. NOW COMES THE TEST OF MAKING IT WORTH THE PRICE OF ADMISSION

The Tigers are 4-2 with wins over Clemson and Texas A&M and are still in the AP top-25 as of this afternoon, falling from 10th to 22nd.

However, this probably isn't how anyone in purple and gold expected the season to go when they imagined the infinite possibilities back in August.

LSU had one of the most expensive rosters in the country, estimated at around $40 million, as well as a coaching staff many considered to be the best in the country, top to bottom.

The loss to Ole Miss three weeks ago stung, but was not unexpected.

The Rebels were favored and had the benefit of playing at home, and the added context of Kiffin returning to the program, he turned his back on to go coach in The Boot made that a tough one to win.

But losing to a first-time head coach at a program that you have a marked talent and resources advantage over is a tough pill to swallow.

WHO'S REALLY PLAYED THE BEST THUS FAR THROUGH THE FIRST HALF OF THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL SEASON?

And to top it all off, the Tigers took a massive L on the recruiting trail on Sunday when their flip target, five-star wide receiver and former Texas commit Easton Royal, opted to head to Gainesville and play for the Gators.

Losing a five-star prospect to an in-conference rival is never fun, but when you consider Royal is from nearby New Orleans and was long thought to be an LSU lean even while committed to the Longhorns, it makes it even harder to accept.

Sure, signing day is still two months away, but that's a prospect you'd rather hold onto than try to flip in the 11th hour.

Things don't get any easier for the Bayou Bengals, either.

Their October features a visit from top-20 Mississippi State as well as a trip to Jordan Hare to play Auburn.

Then they play three consecutive top-15 teams in November (Alabama, Texas, and at Tennessee) before a relative break on the road against Arkansas to end the season.

It's not inconceivable to envision another two losses in that stretch.

If you asked an LSU fan over the summer if 8-4 was an acceptable year one, they would have laughed in your face, and they would have had every right to do so.

Between Kiffin, the coaching staff, and the roster, this is easily a $150 million operation, and 8-4 and a trip to the Duke's Mayo Bowl isn't going to cut the mustard.

Kiffin famously pleaded for patience during spring practice, but unfortunately for him, in this day and age of NIL and the transfer portal, patience no longer exists at a tier one program like LSU.

My confidence in Kiffin's ability to win at LSU has not waned.

First years are rife with trial and error, and not every coach can have a Curt Cignetti-type start to their tenure.

Kiffin and his staff will figure out what works and what doesn't on this roster, and trim the fat where necessary.

As long as the powers that be continue to fund this thing, LSU and Kiffin will be fine.

But Saturday night's loss to Kentucky raises those same uncomfortable questions I already discussed.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Why couldn't a $40 million roster and one of the hottest coaches in the country beat a lower-tier SEC team.

If Will Stein can do it in year one, why can't Lane Kiffin?

I'm not here to answer those questions or even argue their validity, but this is what folks in Baton Rouge will no doubt be thinking this week.

I've said it before, and I will say it again, the honeymoon in Death Valley is over.

Now we get to find out if Kiffin is really made for this gig.

item.title: GOP senator calls for FCC probe of ABC News over Trump sons-Anduril 'political hit job'
item.description: Sen. Bernie Moreno urged the FCC to investigate ABC News over a retracted report linking Donald Trump Jr. and Anduril Industries to government contracts.
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-OH, called on the Federal Communications Commission on Saturday to launch a formal investigation into ABC News after the network deleted and substantially revised a report involving President Donald Trump's sons and defense contractor Anduril Industries, accusing the Disney-owned network of publishing false information that could damage a major investment in his home state.

In a letter to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, Moreno demanded accountability for the network's report and questioned whether ABC News violated its obligations as a broadcaster.

"Thus, I urge the Commission to open a formal investigation into ABC News's political hit job. We must know who signed off on the publication of this false story, who may have asked to profit from the attack, and whether ABC News's conduct violated its obligations as a licensee," Moreno said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Moreno's office for additional comment but a spokesperson for the senator declined to elaborate on the allegations.

FCC CALLS IN DISNEY-OWNED ABC STATIONS FOR EARLY LICENSE REVIEW IN WAKE OF JIMMY KIMMEL CONTROVERSY

The senator's request followed ABC News' decision to remove a report examining investments tied to Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump. The original Wednesday article claimed companies connected to the president's sons had secured billions in government contracts, including through venture capital firm 1789 Capital.

Moreno specifically challenged the original report's characterization of Anduril's financing, arguing that the network had misrepresented the company's investment activity and unfairly associated the Trump family with federal contracting decisions.

"ABC News appears under broadcast licenses issued by the FCC. These licenses are a privilege, not a right. They require service of the public interest," he said.

FCC BOSS BRENDAN CARR MAINTAINS EARLY ABC LICENSE RENEWAL IS ABOUT DEI PROBE, NOT JIMMY KIMMEL CONTROVERSY

The controversy centered on ABC News' original claim that 1789 Capital, where Trump Jr. serves as a partner, acquired a major strike in Anduril through a $2.5 billion investment. The figure instead represented Anduril's broader fundraising round, while 1789 Capital's investment was approximately $50 million.

ABC News republished a substantially revised article Friday, acknowledging errors involving investments, government contracts and the chronology of events. The updated version also clarified that Trump Jr. does not serve on the firm's investment decision-making committee. The report was republished Friday with a new headline, revised byline and an editor's note acknowledging factual errors involving company investments, government contracts and the chronology of events.

Moreno also emphasized the economic stakes for Ohio, where Anduril is developing its Arsenal-1 manufacturing facility. The company has announced plans to invest nearly $1 billion in the project, which is expected to create more than 4,000 jobs.

DISNEY SUES FCC OVER ‘RETALIATORY CAMPAIGN AGAINST ABC,’ SEEKS TO BLOCK EARLY RENEWAL PROCEEDINGS

In his letter, Moreno accused ABC News of undermining public confidence in journalism while potentially harming a major employer in the state.

"The American people, and the workers in Ohio whose jobs were put at risk by this reporting, deserve answers and accountability," Moreno said.

The investigation request comes amid an ongoing legal dispute between Disney and the FCC over the commission's early review of ABC-owned television station licenses. Disney argued that the review threatens constitutionally protected editorial independence, while the FCC defended its actions as regulatory oversight.

Fox News Digital reached out to the FCC but did not immediately receive a response.

A network source for ABC News told Fox News Digital, "We always review every situation in a thorough and thoughtful manner and will not be providing further comment at this time."

item.title: Toddler stabbed in face, suspect previously deemed unfit for trial in attacks on 2 children: report
item.description: Nelson Blanco allegedly stabbed a toddler at a Rhode Island school bus stop, decades after being found incompetent to stand trial for knifing two boys.
item.content:encoded:
A stranger allegedly stabbed a toddler in the face as she sat in her stroller at a Rhode Island school bus stop, years after he was accused of knifing two other children and found incompetent to stand trial.

The child’s fight for survival has brought renewed scrutiny into the suspect’s past, including an attack on two children more than two decades ago and repeated findings that he was incompetent to stand trial.

Nelson Blanco, 46, is accused of stabbing the 2-year-old girl and her mother Wednesday afternoon near Broad and Public streets in Providence, police said.

SOUTH CAROLINA MOM ACCUSED OF KNIFE ATTACK ON YOUNG CHILDREN; 6-YEAR-OLD MAY LOSE ARM: SHERIFF'S OFFICE

The toddler was taken to Hasbro Children’s Hospital in critical condition. Her mother, who suffered a stab wound to the shoulder, was treated and released, according to local reporting.

The mother was waiting with her daughter for her other children to get off a school bus when Blanco allegedly approached and made insulting comments, Providence Police Chief Oscar Perez said, according to WPRI.

ANGEL MOM SAYS BLUE STATE DAS ARE PUTTING ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CRIMINALS BEFORE PUBLIC SAFETY

She crossed the street with the stroller to get away, but Blanco approached again and allegedly attacked the child with a knife, police said, noting there was no evidence he knew either victim.

Surveillance video showed the mother and daughter attempting to move away before Blanco grabbed the stroller and struck the child repeatedly, Boston 25 News reported.

A bystander tried to intervene, but Blanco allegedly attempted to stab that person before fleeing, according to the outlet.

Officers found Blanco hiding in the basement of a nearby home and recovered a knife from a panel box, police said. Authorities said he admitted to the stabbings during questioning.

CALIFORNIA STABBING VICTIM'S FRIEND BLASTS 'FAILED' JUSTICE SYSTEM OVER ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT SUSPECT'S RELEASE

Blanco allegedly told detectives he stopped the attack because he was on a main street, according to a police report obtained by WPRI.

"If I was on a side street, I would have killed them. Both of them," he said, according to the outlet.

PROSECUTORS SAY CHARLOTTE TRAIN STABBING CASE WON'T BE DISMISSED REGARDLESS OF COMPETENCY RULING

Blanco faces six charges, including two counts police identified as assault with intent to commit murder, felony assault, breaking and entering into an occupied dwelling of a person 60 or older, and two weapons charges.

No plea was entered during his Thursday appearance in Rhode Island’s 6th Division District Court. The court referred him to the public defender and requested an evaluation, according to court records reviewed by Fox News Digital.

VIOLENT TRANSIT ATTACKS IN ATLANTA, NEW YORK AND CHARLOTTE FUEL CALLS FOR TOUGHER TRACKING OF REPEAT OFFENDERS

WPRI reported Blanco is being held without bail pending a competency hearing later this month.

His arrest brought back painful memories for Andy Lopez and Dave Belony, who told WPRI they were 6 and 7 years old when Blanco attacked them while they played in Lopez’s backyard on Sept. 27, 2003.

CHARLOTTE REPEAT OFFENDER CHARGED WITH KILLING MAN HOURS AFTER RELEASE ON BOND

Belony said he recognized Blanco immediately when he saw his booking photo on social media Wednesday night.

"I knew it was him, because I will always remember that face," he told the station. "My heart dropped, and it truly felt like my world had stopped."

Court records reviewed by Fox News Digital show Blanco faced two felony assault charges and a charge of possessing a knife or firearm during a crime, stemming from the 2003 incident.

BANK OF AMERICA EXEC KILLED IN RANDOM TIMES SQUARE STABBING LAID TO REST AS HUNDREDS MOURN YOUNG MOM

The docket documents repeated findings that Blanco was incompetent to stand trial from September 2004 through March 2006. Multiple entries state, "Defendant Remains Incompetent." The case remains listed as "under review" in the court portal.

More recently, Blanco was found incompetent to stand trial in July in a separate domestic violence case, WPRI reported. A judge accepted a doctor’s recommendation allowing him to remain in outpatient treatment because he was considered unlikely to endanger the community or himself at that time.

Lopez and Belony said the earlier attack left them with injuries and trauma that have followed them into adulthood.

They told WPRI they were playing with Lopez’s brother when Blanco emerged from a shed behind the house where he had been living.

"He didn’t say a word," Belony recalled. "His face was blank and he was just staring at us."

Belony said Blanco charged at him, trapping him near a tree. He curled into a ball and covered his head as Blanco stabbed him.

DEMOCRATIC BOSTON COUNCILOR RIPS 'SOFT-ON-CRIME' POLICIES AFTER SUSPECTED GUNMAN'S VIOLENT PAST REVEALED

Blanco then turned toward Lopez, the men said.

"My brother yelled at me to run, and I was trying to run but my body just froze," Lopez told WPRI. "He stabbed me twice in the eye — the first time it was blurry, and then the second time I couldn’t see anything."

Both children were rushed to Hasbro Children’s Hospital. Their recovery took three months and included at least three surgeries each, they told the outlet.

Lopez was left permanently blind in his left eye, an injury he said derailed his dreams of becoming a police officer or truck driver.

"Most of the opportunities I wanted to have in life are gone," he said. "I’m very grateful I’m alive, but my life is restricted."

Belony said he was stabbed at least five times in his stomach, back and ribs and continues to struggle emotionally.

The men said learning about the latest attack left them devastated for the mother and toddler, and determined to speak out.

"It’s frustrating for us, not only because of what happened to us, but because it has happened to others," Lopez told WPRI. "He was given a chance 23 years ago, and 23 years later, he did the same thing."

"We want justice for the victims," Belony said. "What is it going to take for him to be held accountable for his actions?"

Fox News Digital reached out to the Providence Police Department and the Rhode Island attorney general’s office for comment.

item.title: 'I lost us that game': Nick Sirianni makes decision that opened door to a Jacksonville Jaguars comeback win
item.description: Nick Sirianni says he cost the Eagles the game after a short kickoff let the Jaguars set up Cam Little's stunning walk-off 57-yard field goal.
item.content:encoded:
NFL head coaches often take responsibility for not helping their team, but usually when they seek the blame for losing, they are often covering for someone else's mistake. Then we have Philadelphia Eagles coach Nick Sirianni.

He took the blame for the Eagles' walk-off field goal loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars on Sunday because, well, it was indeed ultimately on him.

Why?

Because the Eagles blew the game in London by not kicking the ball into the end zone while clinging to a 17-16 lead with only eight seconds to play.

JALEN HURTS CURSES AT RECEIVER IN VIRAL HOT-MIC MOMENT DURING EAGLES' COLLAPSE AGAINST RAMS

Down two points, the Jaguars returned the kick that was short of the end zone 53 yards to the Eagles' 39-yard line. The runback took seven seconds.

And with one second remaining left, Cam Little, who has a kicking leg like a howitzer, connected on a game-winning 57-yard field goal.

That left the Eagles with their third loss of the season.

And Sirianni with mushy peas on his face.

"I lost us that game and that's what I said to our guys," Sirianni admitted in his post-game news conference.

"What hurt there is that the guys fought so hard, and I don’t make the decision that I should make at the end of the game and I cost us that game, and I put that fully on me."

Sirianni was not in the mood to accept other reasons the Eagles lost.

"At the end of the day, I didn’t make the right decision, and it cost us the game," he said. "You know, and so there’s no other way around it. There’s nothing really else to say about that. It’s just I didn’t do my job good enough in that situation."

It was obviously not all Sirianni's fault. The Eagles' kickoff coverage unit was leaky from the start of the game to the end.

And maybe kicker Jake Elliott should have kicked the ball into the end zone of his own accord. He is a veteran and should understand the situation.

But, people in Philly, raise your hand if you disagree that Sirianni had a brain lock.

Waiting for a hand to rise.

Still waiting.

Nobody.

Sirianni is going to carry this for a while because Eagles fans are not too forgiving. And neither is the Philadelphia media.

"It’s just like you would feel if you missed a free throw at the end of the game, or if you had a drop," Sirianni said. "I’ve been in both of those places. And those ones stick with you, and that will stick with me for a long time.

"... Yeah, that one will hurt for a long time. I still think about those other things that have, I’ve lost games for us in the past as far as, you know, when I played."

MIKE TOMLIN POINTS OUT DALLAS COWBOYS 'NEGLIGENT' COACHING MISTAKES AND PUT HIMSELF IN CONVERSATION TO TAKE JOB NEXT YEAR

There are two issues with what Sirianni just said:

First, it is the coach's job to stop the bleeding. His team already allowed a fourth-quarter loss to the Rams last week to become a two-week disaster and grow into a three-game losing skid overall.

Second, if Sirianni's message to his team is that this loss will stick with him a long time, that is exactly the wrong message to send.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

What's up with these NFC East coaches?

A couple of weeks ago, the Dallas Cowboys blew a game against the Baltimore Ravens in the final seconds when coach Brian Schottenheimer didn't order a kickoff rocketed into the end zone.

The crazy part of this is that Sirianni says he saw that situation on tape.

"I watched a ton of those situations after that Dallas game and, again, just didn’t make the right decision in this particular case," he said.

item.title: Mojtaba Khamenei defies ‘malicious’ attacks as US Army zeroes in on Iran’s 350,000 troops
item.description: Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei claimed U.S. and Israeli strikes failed to weaken Iran's military, as the U.S. Army released a new threat guide.
item.content:encoded:
Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei claimed Oct. 8 that U.S. and Israeli strikes had failed to undermine Iran's domestic security forces, praising police personnel for resisting attacks launched in February under Operations Epic Fury and Roaring Lion.

Khamenei's remarks on X also came as the U.S. Army released a new battlefield identification guide to help American troops recognize members of Iran's conventional military, known as the Artesh, whose ground forces were estimated by the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security in June at 350,000 personnel.

"The criminal US-Zionist enemy's desperate efforts and malicious attacks on the pillars of social order and security, which are unparalleled throughout history, have not caused the courageous personnel of the Police Force to waver even a fraction in their mission," Khamenei wrote in a statement.

Khamenei specifically praised Iran's Law Enforcement Command, known as FARAJA, accusing the United States and Israel of targeting the institution responsible for maintaining domestic order.

"The focus and persistence of the criminal US-Zionist enemy in striking at the Police Force at its various levels, from its highest command levels down to those who are on the frontline, has only served to underscore the paramount importance of this institution more than ever," he wrote.

IRAN PROVES THAT IT MIGHT CHANGE ITS MILITARY LEADERS, BUT IT’S NOT CHANGING STRATEGY

Iran's security apparatus comprises three principal branches: the Artesh, responsible primarily for conventional territorial defense; the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), tasked with protecting the Islamic Republic and projecting military power; and FARAJA, responsible for domestic law enforcement and internal security.

IRAN’S GUTTED RANKS LEAVE LOYALISTS FILLING CRITICAL POSTS — WITH ONE GLARING PROBLEM

FARAJA, commanded by Brig. Gen. Ahmadreza Radan, is responsible for maintaining public order, enforcing the country's laws and responding to civil unrest.

According to Iran Human Rights Monitor, the force has evolved into a powerful internal security institution involved in suppressing anti-government demonstrations, monitoring political activity and enforcing the regime's ideological restrictions.

IRAN INSTALLS NEW WAR CHIEFS AS TEHRAN SIGNALS ‘PROLONGED CONFRONTATION,’ EXPERT WARNS

Radan has also been sanctioned by the United States for his role in human rights abuses.

The Treasury Department designated him in September 2010, citing his responsibility for beatings, killings and arbitrary arrests of protesters following Iran's disputed 2009 presidential election.

Khamenei also called for strengthening FARAJA on Oct. 8 through additional personnel, equipment and technology, including the use of artificial intelligence for data analysis.

AFTER 47 YEARS OF CONFRONTING IRAN, DOES AMERICA HAVE A STRATEGY FOR ENDING THIS WAR?

His remarks come as the U.S. Army's Training and Transformation Command published a "Know the Threat" recognition guide Sept. 24, highlighted by Defense News on Oct. 9.

The guide shows an Iranian special forces soldier and identifies weapons American troops could encounter, including AKM rifles, Iranian-made Masaf-2 rifles, German-designed G3 rifles, MG3 machine guns and RPG-7 rocket-propelled grenade launchers.

The Artesh, Iran's regular military, is separate from the IRGC and its affiliated Basij militia. Its forces operate across four branches: the Ground Forces, Navy, Air Force and Air Defense Force.

A June assessment by the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security estimated the Artesh's Ground Forces at approximately 350,000 personnel, including 220,000 conscripts.

The report found that the Artesh had suffered severe losses across its air, naval and air defense components during the opening phase of the U.S.-Israeli military campaign, while its ground forces remained structurally intact because there had been no ground invasion.

TRUMP OPENS HORMUZ UNDER FIRE WITH ‘PROJECT FREEDOM’ AS IRAN WARNS OF ATTACKS

The Artesh is commanded by Maj. Gen. Amir Hatami, a former Iranian defense minister who assumed command in June 2025.

Aside from Khamenei, Hatami issued his own warning Oct. 6, claiming Iran's adversaries faced "historic confusion" after failing to halt military production during the conflict.

Hatami also claimed that Iranian defense production continued despite American and Israeli attacks, saying the country's military production lines had continued operating during the conflict.

The extent of Iran's military recovery remains unclear. The Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security assessed in June that the country's conventional air, naval and air defense forces had suffered severe damage during the conflict.

President Donald Trump, meanwhile, said Oct. 8 that Washington would not resume military strikes against Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, citing "productive discussions" between the two countries.

item.title: Luxury hotel favored by Kennedys, Grace Kelly cracks down on influencer photo shoots
item.description: The famed Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc on the French Riviera bans photo shoots without permission as influencers and social media habits clash with guest privacy at the luxury property.
item.content:encoded:
A well-known luxury hotel is cracking down on photo shoots and cellphone use as some visitors' social media habits clash with other guests' desire for privacy.

Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc has introduced rules aimed at limiting disruptive photography and preserving privacy at the property.

The famed hotel on the French Riviera in Antibes, France, has long attracted prominent guests — with members of the Kennedy family among those who have spent time in its rooms, suites and villas. 

ONCE-HIDDEN COASTAL TOWN FACING DISRUPTION AS SOCIAL MEDIA INFLUENCERS TRANSFORM LOCAL LIFE

Grace Kelly, Orson Welles, Elizabeth Taylor, F. Scott Fitzgerald, Ernest Hemingway, Cole Porter and Pablo Picasso are among the others who would also frequent the property.

The hotel has also hosted high-profile celebrations, including the 2023 wedding of Sofia Richie Grainge, daughter of musician Lionel Richie.

Under the hotel's current policy, photo shoots are prohibited on the property unless guests receive permission from management.

"To preserve the peace and privacy of all our guests, photo shoots are not permitted on the property," the hotel states on its website.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Guests with special photography requests are directed to the hotel's concierge, who can review the request and, when appropriate, connect people with the property's photographer, according to the website.

The restrictions come amid growing concerns over how some visitors are using the hotel, according to Travel Weekly.

Hotel manager Sophie Volant told the outlet that some people visiting for lunch were spending more time taking photos than enjoying their meals.

"We have a lot of loyal, repeat guests who don't see this hotel as a hotel — they see Hotel du Cap as their summer home," said Volant.

item.title: Will Stein's dad storms the field after Kentucky's upset win over LSU in beautiful college football scene
item.description: Video captures Will Stein's father slowly walking onto the field with arms raised as Kentucky fans stormed the turf after the overtime upset of LSU.
item.content:encoded:
There were quite a few happy people in Lexington, Kentucky, on Saturday night after the Wildcats upset LSU in an overtime thriller, but it's hard to imagine anyone being happier than Will Stein's father, and there is video evidence to support it.

After LSU needed just two plays to score on its first possession in overtime to jump out to a 34-27 lead, the Wildcats were forced to respond, and respond they did. Running back CJ Baxter punched it into the end zone, which left Stein with a decision to make: kick the extra point and head into a second overtime or go for two and try to end the game in front of your home crowd.

Stein opted for the latter, and it paid off.

KENTUCKY COACH WILL STEIN TELLS WILDCATS PLAYERS 'IF YOU DON'T BELIEVE IN WHAT WE'RE DOING, YOU ARE HIGH'

After a controversial flag on the first two-point conversion that was negated by a Kentucky timeout, quarterback Kenny Minchey trotted onto the field and walked right up the middle into the end zone to send Big Blue Nation into a frenzy with a 35-34 victory.

It was Kentucky's second consecutive 35-34 overtime win after the Wildcats came back to win at South Carolina seven days prior.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Given the win over the No. 10 team in the nation and it marking Kentucky's first victory over LSU in Lexington since 2007, fans celebrated accordingly and stormed the field.

As thousands of Kentucky fans leaped over the walls of the stadium and sprinted onto the turf, Stein's father got in on the fun as well, but in a different fashion.

Surrounded by pure and joyful chaos, Stein slowly walked onto the turf with his arms in the air in awe of the scene unfolding in front of him.

Each college football season creates its own set of magical moments, but a father basking in a moment his son just managed to pull off at the school he grew up being a die-hard fan of is about as special as it gets.

Stein rushed the field when Kentucky upset LSU in 2007, and for him to deliver another field storm as the Wildcats newest head coach against the same team in front of his old man is objectively awesome.

item.title: Sydney Sweeney doubles down with topless sports betting ad weeks after backlash: ‘I’m flattered’
item.description: Sydney Sweeney's new Novig ad shows the "Euphoria" star ditching her top and covering herself with footballs amid fierce women in sports backlash.
item.content:encoded:
Sydney Sweeney is doubling down on her controversial Novig sports betting ads.

On Sunday, the "Euphoria" star ditched her top in a new commercial for the prediction market platform, wearing only white Novig underwear while strategically covering herself with footballs.

"There are grown men making spreadsheets to bet on what color underwear I’m wearing," Sweeney says in the ad posted on Instagram. "I mean, I’m flattered?"

SYDNEY SWEENEY’S PROVOCATIVE SPORTS AD 'REINFORCES THE IMAGE SHE HAS ALREADY BUILT' DESPITE BACKLASH: EXPERT

She then jokes about someone "betting their 401(k) on a war" before concluding, "Novig is … just sports."

The new campaign comes weeks after Sweeney’s first Novig advertisement sparked fierce backlash from female athletes and critics who accused the company of sexualizing women in sports.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Sweeney’s latest post quickly drew support from fans, with commenters writing, "Keep going girl," and, "Here comes the wave of angry people."

EXCLUSIVE: STAR FEMALE GOLFER FIRES BACK AT SYDNEY SWEENEY CRITICS: 'SHE'S GOT SEX APPEAL'

In the original ad, Sweeney appeared nearly nude while posing with sports equipment and telling viewers the platform was "just sports." The campaign prompted criticism from Olympians and professional athletes, including swimmer Ariarne Titmus, who called it a "kick in the face" to women who have devoted their lives to sports.

SHARON STONE TELLS SYDNEY SWEENEY TO 'TAKE RESPONSIBILITY' FOR PROVOCATIVE SPORTS AD

Gymnast Gracie Kramer accused the ad of marketing women’s sports "through the male gaze," while British sprinter Amy Hunt said the campaign offered an inaccurate picture of what women in sports look like.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SAYS WHAT OTHER GASLIGHTING FEMALE ATHLETES WON'T ABOUT THE NAKED SYDNEY SWEENEY AD

Sweeney later appeared to respond by sharing images of famous athletes, including Serena Williams, Ronda Rousey, Sue Bird, Megan Rapinoe and Caroline Wozniacki, who had posed nude for ESPN’s Body Issue.

Adrienne Uthe, founder of Kronus Communications, previously told Fox News Digital that while Sweeney's ad may have ruffled feathers, "women having agency also means allowing women to make choices about their image that other women may not personally agree with."

"People are entitled to dislike the ad, just like women athletes are entitled to criticize it for their own reasons," Uthe said. "But I don't think this is materially damaging to Sydney Sweeney in any way, shape or form.

"In fact, I don't think it's a large departure from who she is and what her brand represents. She's a beautiful woman right now at the peak of her career, and she ultimately can decide which projects she wants to take and which ones she doesn't."

BROADCAST BIAS: MEDIA BASH SYDNEY SWEENEY, BUT COVER FOR LEFTIST MACKLEMORE

She added, "And she's chosen to make sexuality a part of her brand for better or for worse."

Novig defended the original advertisement as a "fun idea" created with "confidence, humor and a playful edge."

The latest campaign is not the first time Sweeney has found herself at the center of a major advertising controversy.

In 2025, her American Eagle campaign, titled "Sydney Sweeney Has Great Jeans," drew backlash over a promotional video that played on the words "genes" and "jeans." Critics accused the campaign of carrying racial undertones, with some social media users even labeling it "Nazi propaganda."

Other fans defended Sweeney and the clothing brand, arguing that the ad was simply a playful promotion for jeans. One supporter wrote, "Woke advertising is dead. Sydney Sweeney killed it."

item.title: In Springfield, Ohio, Trump must settle the MAGA vs Chamber of Commerce war
item.description: Springfield, Ohio, small business owners reveal what they need from Vivek Ramaswamy and John Husted on taxes, regulations, and immigration reform.
item.content:encoded:
At a rally in Ohio last week, President Donald Trump told his supporters that, "Even if you hate John Husted, even if you hate Vivek Ramaswamy, you have to go vote for them." It was a blunt assessment of the GOP’s respective candidates for Senate and governor, but one that Trump, who wins Ohio elections like Tom Brady won Super Bowls, knows is vitally important.

Trump would laugh off the remark, saying that nobody really hates the GOP candidates. But he was making an essential point, especially in Ohio, which is the front line of the war between the traditional GOP and Trump’s MAGA base, much of it centered on the question of immigration.

To hear from the Chamber of Commerce side, I spoke with Jim Lagos, who has lived his entire 75 years in Springfield, owns several buildings downtown, and has been a central figure in the attempts to revitalize the city’s downtown district.

TRUMP TOUTS ‘GOLDEN AGE’ AT OHIO RALLY, URGES VOTERS TO DELIVER GOP MIDTERM WINS

"You have to pull the trigger," Jim told me of efforts to bring the very pretty, but very empty downtown back to life. "My father always used to tell me 'Christopher Columbus took a risk.'"

Jim, as is customary for civic leaders, had nice things to say about Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown and gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, both of whom he has met. But he is all in for Husted and even more so for Ramasamy, who he hopes will slash regulations to speed up the recovery of towns like Springfield.

RAMASWAMY OUTLINES KEY CONTRASTS WITH DEM OPPONENT LESS THAN 100 DAYS OUT FROM KEY GUBERNATORIAL ELECTION

"We have temporary cuts on taxes for small business in Ohio," Jim said. "But they need to be extended. Big companies got a permanent break, because they are smart enough to donate to both parties."

Over the past three decades, Jim has rehabilitated several historic buildings in Springfield and succeeded in filling most of the space with occupants.

"Sometimes, when business is struggling, you have to carry them for a while until it gets better," he said.

ICE PREPARES MAJOR OPERATION TARGETING HAITIANS LOSING TPS AFTER SUPREME COURT RULING

The issue that most bitterly divides the business leaders in Springfield from the MAGA base of Trump voters in the area is immigration, and in particular, the wave of 15,000 Haitian refugees who arrived between 2020 and 2025, overwhelming schools, housing stock, and even the Bureau of Motor Vehicles, according to locals.

Jim admits that the messaging, including the idea that Haitian migrants are better workers who don’t do drugs and want overtime, not only missed the mark, but downright offended many local native residents.

Ramaswamy has, in the past veered toward a similar sentiment, which Frank, who works construction in the area, took some issue with.

"I don’t like his idea that immigrants are, like, making us better from competition, I’d rather put Americans first," Frank said.

According to Walter Curt, an investigative journalist who lives in Springfield, "When Trump came to office the first time, a bunch of factories got built in the area, and as soon as Biden got in, he staffed them with Haitians, effectively," through tax breaks to temp companies and business owners.

DEM SENATE CANDIDATE SHERROD BROWN CLAIMS HE SUPPORTS 'CLOSING THE BORDER'; GOP SAYS RECORD PROVES OTHERWISE

Importantly, while Curt does hold current Ohio governor and well known loather of President Trump, Mike DeWine, culpable for the Haitian situation, he does not blame the Haitians themselves, or Husted or Ramaswamy.

"The entire country of Haiti would be in his front yard [Ohio] if it was up to DeWine," Curt said. "If anybody believes Vivek is of the same mind, I haven’t seen any evidence of that."

AMERICA NEEDS WORKERS, BUT TRUMP'S POLICIES ARE SHARPLY CUTTING LEGAL IMMIGRATION

Further complicating the immigration issue in Springfield is the fact that there is a largely Hispanic immigrant population well integrated into and assimilated with the broader community, something one does not see with the Haitian refugees.

Victoria and Ambrosio opened Food Fusion, a large eatery with great food, a year ago, and they employ a mix of native born Springfielders as well as immigrants from Mexico, a dynamic you also see with the clientele.

SMALL BUSINESS OWNERS BUILT THE AMERICAN DREAM. DEMOCRATS WANT TO TAKE IT FROM YOU

What these first-time restaurant owners want from government is more transparency about regulations.

"You don’t know everything that comes with it," Victoria told me. "As far as taxes, you have to know this, you have have to know that, and not just the rules and regulations of liquor licenses. There’s really no help for small business owners."

Trump is correct that the vast majority of Republican voters in Ohio don’t hate Husted or Ramaswamy. Many downright love them. But in a close midterm race, the GOP needs those who don’t.

DAVID MARCUS: IN DAYTON, OHIO, BOTH PARTIES FACE BITTER POLITICAL DESPONDENCY

The battle between MAGA and the Chamber for the soul of the GOP is not just an Ohio story. it will be the story of the next two years as Republicans seek a new standard bearer.

item.title: Kourtney Kardashian's expletive-filled reaction to Oscar-winning actress calling her 'annoying'
item.description: Kourtney Kardashian fired back at an Oscar-winning actress on "The Kardashians" premiere, threatening to "slap the s--- out of her" before an apology arrived.
item.content:encoded:
Kourtney Kardashian had some choice words for Jennifer Lawrence after the Oscar-winning actress called her "more annoying than ever" and said she "drives me nuts" during a 2025 Vanity Fair lie-detector interview.

Kardashian addressed the remarks during the season 8 premiere of "The Kardashians," revealing that Lawrence later apologized by email.

The drama began when Lawrence was asked which member of the Kardashian family was her favorite. She selected Khloé Kardashian and then criticized Kourtney’s behavior on the reality show.

Lawrence also said Kourtney "drives me nuts" and was "more annoying than ever."

Kourtney, 47, said she was particularly upset after her mother, Kris Jenner, mentioned spending time with Lawrence and Emma Stone.
